achado: Plastic debris found in the stomachs of 28% of individuals (34.6% estuarine; 19.2% marine); packaging items in 64.3% and fishing-gear fragments in 35.7%. No ulcerations or obstructions recorded.

Anthropogenic particles present in 100% of intestinal samples; 99% fibres (polyester, polypropylene, acrylic, polyethylene) plus manufactured pigments; evidence suggestive of uptake into the intestinal wall.
Most individuals contained plastic in stomach contents; PU, PET and EVA were the predominant polymers; microplastics outnumbered meso- and macroplastics.
Fragment-type microplastics in the intestines of all individuals; meso- or macroplastics in 4 of 12, including a 19.2 cm polypropylene item traced to a source ~943 km away.
Plastic ingestion recorded in 1 of 23 individuals (a seabird); none of the marine mammals examined contained plastic.
Whistle duration decreased, and whistle rate increased, with ambient noise level, indicating that noise modifies acoustic communication.
Dolphins overlapped with boats in deeper areas but, at finer spatial scales, preferentially used areas of lower boat traffic.
Priority habitat for blue whales overlaps with maritime traffic routes, implying collision and noise exposure risk.
Cetacean distribution overlaps with shipping traffic within the Humboldt Current System.
A seismological network was successfully used to detect and localise Bryde's whale calls (acoustic monitoring tool).
POPs and contaminants of emerging concern detected in 37 blubber samples, at levels well below those reported for the Indian and Pacific oceans.
Organohalogen profiles changed after the 2015 Fundão tailings-dam collapse; pesticide concentrations increased after 2015.
Bycatch and mining-derived metal pollution identified as the principal threats; metals analysed in muscle and skin of five individuals.
The piracatinga fishery uses river-dolphin carcasses as bait; the fish exceeds the WHO mercury limit (0.5 µg/g), threatening dolphins and human consumers alike.
Debris present in 10.1% of 884 stranded cetaceans (22 species), 2015–2020; the franciscana showed the highest ingestion rate (17.9%). Gross digestive lesions were rare.
Microplastics (PP, PE, PET, PS, nylon, acrylates, polycarbonates) detected in two stranded Guiana dolphins and in sea turtles; the first plastic record for cetaceans in French Guiana.
At least 45 charismatic marine species interact with plastics in the region; the franciscana is proposed as one of eight indicator species of plastic pollution.
Sound exposure level was the main predictor of reduced whistle rate (52.4% contribution); dolphins used noisy areas but communicated mainly in quieter ones.

area: Rio de Janeiro coast and Vitória-Trindade Seamount Chain
achado: One month of passive acoustic monitoring: coastal Rio de Janeiro showed higher sound levels than the oceanic site; low-frequency cetaceans were the most exposed hearing group.
None of the licensing reports for port construction and seismic activity assessed impacts on cetacean acoustics; 59.6% relied solely on literature review.
Only Brazil and Peru had statutory guidelines to mitigate seismic-survey impacts; EIAs were mandatory in 11 countries, but monitoring and mitigation were generally weak.
Fin whales from the Sea of Cortez showed lower PBT chemical burdens, plastic additives and biomarker responses than Mediterranean whales.
